question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
(x-6)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={(x-6)}^{2}{y}^{3/4}.
$$

Work on an interval where $x-6>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined. Take $y>0$.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-6)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={(x-6)}^{2}{y}^{3/4} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{y}{(x-6)} & =(x-6){y}^{3/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={(x-6)}^{-1},\,q(x)=(x-6),\,n=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3/4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3/4}\frac{dy}{dx}+{(x-6)}^{-1}{y}^{1/4}=(x-6).\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/4}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-3/4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3/4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{(x-6)}^{-1}z=(x-6)
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-1}z=\frac{(x-6)}{4}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{4\cdot (x-6)},\,Q(x)=\frac{(x-6)}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (\frac{1}{4\cdot (x-6)})\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(1/4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-6)} \\  & ={(x-6)}^{1/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={(x-6)}^{1/4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-1}z) & ={(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot (\frac{(x-6)}{4}) \\ {(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-3/4}z & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{(x-6)}^{1/4}) & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{(x-6)}^{1/4})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{(x-6)}^{1/4} & =\frac{1}{9}{(x-6)}^{9/4}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=9{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/4}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{1/4}=\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}}\,⇒\,y={(\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}})}^{4}\,.
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above. Since $z=y^{1/4}>0$, retain only intervals where the displayed expression for $z$ is positive.

generation.domains: translated coordinate positive; nonzero real branches; exclude singularities
